issues.legal_issue: The property-disclosure and solvency/security requirements do not apply to a sale covering shops in multiple tehsils when the required assessment cannot be made through a single tehsildar.
material_facts: The sale covered shops situated in nineteen tehsils.
The requirements contemplated one tehsildar reviewing the purchaser’s property statement and assessing solvency and the value of security.
The rules provided no process for reconciling conflicting assessments by multiple tehsildars.
issues.conclusion: The property-statement requirement and the related solvency and security-assessment requirements did not apply to this sale, so the purchaser was not required to comply with them.
issues.legal_principle: The court construed rule 19(1), (3) and (4) of the Mysore Excise (Disposal of Privileges of Retail Vend of Liquors) Rules, 1967 in light of the duties assigned to 'the tahsildar' and the absence of any mechanism for multiple tahsildars to make or reconcile the relevant findings. It held that these provisions did not apply where the shops were situated in two or more tehsils.

predicates.challenge_to_excise_sale_cancellation: A purchaser challenged the cancellation of a sale of retail liquor-vending rights.
predicates.shops_span_multiple_local_jurisdictions: The shops covered by the sale were situated in more than one local jurisdiction.
predicates.assessment_framework_requires_one_local_: The required property review and solvency or security assessment were assigned to a single local officer, with no process for reconciling assessments by multiple officers.

issues.definition: When a purchaser challenges cancellation of a sale covering shops in multiple local jurisdictions and the assessment framework requires one local officer, the property-disclosure and related security requirements do not apply.

issues.legal_issue: An application for a licence made 'at once' means an application made within a reasonable time before the licensed business is due to commence.
material_facts: The licensed business was required to commence on July 1.
The purchaser applied to the excise commissioner for permission to obtain licences and later applied to the divisional commissioner for the licences before July 1.
The purchaser's applications left time for the licences to be issued before business commenced.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser sufficiently complied with the requirement to apply 'at once' for licences.
issues.legal_principle: The court interpreted rule 19(1) of the Mysore Excise (Disposal of Privileges of Retail Vend of Liquors) Rules, 1967 purposively, together with the requirement under the Mysore Excise Licences (General Conditions) Rules, 1967 that the licensee commence business on July 1. 'At once' meant within a reasonable time before that commencement date, rather than immediately after the sale.

predicates.challenge_to_excise_sale_cancellation: A purchaser challenged the cancellation of a sale of retail liquor-vending rights.
predicates.application_made_before_business_start: The purchaser applied for the required licences before the licensed business was due to commence.
predicates.sufficient_time_remained_for_licence_iss: The application was made with enough time for the licences to be issued before the business was due to commence.

issues.definition: When a purchaser challenging cancellation applies before the business is due to commence and enough time remains to issue the licences, the application satisfies the requirement to apply promptly.

issues.legal_issue: A divisional commissioner cannot revise his own order confirming a sale or exercise the authority assigned to the excise commissioner to order forfeiture.
material_facts: The divisional commissioner had confirmed the purchaser's highest bid.
The same divisional commissioner later cancelled the sale for alleged non-compliance with licensing requirements.
The excise commissioner and the state government had not revised the confirmation, and the divisional commissioner did not have authority to order forfeiture.
issues.conclusion: The divisional commissioner lacked authority to cancel the confirmed sale or order forfeiture, and the cancellation was invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Under rule 17(2) of the Mysore Excise (Disposal of Privileges of Retail Vend of Liquors) Rules, 1967, only the excise commissioner or the state government could revise the divisional commissioner's confirmation of a sale. The court also held that the divisional commissioner was not competent to make an order under rule 20(2) forfeiting deposits; that authority lay with the excise commissioner.

predicates.challenge_to_excise_sale_cancellation: A purchaser challenged the cancellation of a sale of retail liquor-vending rights.
predicates.confirming_officer_cancelled_own_confirm: The officer who confirmed the sale later purported to cancel that same sale.
predicates.no_authorized_authority_revised_confirma: No authority empowered to revise the confirmation had revised it before the cancellation.

issues.definition: When a purchaser challenges a cancellation made by the officer who confirmed the sale and no authorized authority has revised that confirmation, the cancellation is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative circular cannot alter or displace a binding rule when the issuing authority lacks power to amend that rule.
material_facts: The excise commissioner issued a circular prescribing an alternative procedure for deposits and security while awaiting clarification from the state government.
The circular's alternative procedure differed from the requirements of the applicable rules.
The excise commissioner had no power to abrogate or modify a rule made under the statutory rule-making power.
issues.conclusion: The circular was ineffective to the extent that it attempted to modify the rules.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that the excise commissioner could not abrogate or modify a rule framed under section 71 of the Mysore Excise Act, 1965 by issuing a circular. It expressed no opinion on whether the commissioner could issue general instructions in matters not covered by the rules.

rule.if: dispute_over_excise_administrative_circular and executive_official_issued_circular and circular_changes_binding_rule and official_lacks_rule_amending_authority

predicates.dispute_over_excise_administrative_circu: A dispute concerned whether an administrative circular governed compliance with excise requirements.
predicates.executive_official_issued_circular: An executive official issued a circular prescribing a procedure.
predicates.circular_changes_binding_rule: The circular prescribed a procedure that differed from a binding rule.
predicates.official_lacks_rule_amending_authority: The issuing official lacked authority to amend or displace the binding rule.

issues.definition: When an official without rule-amending authority issues a circular that changes a binding rule, the circular cannot modify that rule.

issues.legal_issue: A bidder is not established to be acting for an undisclosed purchaser merely because the bidder obtained financing from others.
material_facts: A rival bidder alleged that the purchaser was a benamidar and that accepting the bid was prohibited.
The purchaser was a retired inspector with limited personal income but had access to substantial funds from financiers.
No particular person was identified as the real purchaser, and the evidence did not establish that another person managed the shops or sold liquor.
The rival bidder bore the burden of proving the alleged benami purchase.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not establish that the purchaser was a benamidar or that the bid contravened the prohibition on bidding for another person.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 12 of the Mysore Excise (Disposal of Privileges of Retail Vend of Liquors) Rules, 1967 prohibited a person from bidding for another except as a power-of-attorney holder. The burden of proving a benami purchase rested on the party alleging it, and financing from others alone did not prove that the bidder was a benamidar. Sections 15 and 26 of the Mysore Excise Act, 1965 were relevant to the contention that an unlicensed real buyer's sale of liquor would be illegal. The court distinguished Venkata Subbayya v. Attar Sheik Mastan, A.I.R. 1949 Mad. 252, because the alleged benami purchase and unlawful operation by another person were not established on the evidence.

rule.if: challenge_to_accepted_excise_bid and rival_alleges_undisclosed_real_purchaser and bidder_received_financing_from_others and no_evidence_identifies_real_purchaser_or_shows_other_person_operated_business

predicates.challenge_to_accepted_excise_bid: A party challenged the acceptance of a bid for retail liquor-vending rights.
predicates.rival_alleges_undisclosed_real_purchaser: A rival bidder alleged that the successful bidder acted for another person.
predicates.bidder_received_financing_from_others: The successful bidder obtained funds or financial backing from other people.
predicates.no_evidence_identifies_real_purchaser_or: The evidence did not identify another person as the real purchaser or show that another person managed the business or sold the goods.

issues.definition: When a rival challenges an accepted bid by alleging an undisclosed purchaser, financing from others without evidence identifying that purchaser or showing that the other person operated the business does not establish a benami bid.

issues.legal_issue: The next-highest bid cannot be accepted under the rule for rejected highest bids after the highest bid has been accepted; a later reversal requires a fresh disposal.
material_facts: The officer conducting the sale accepted the purchaser's highest offer, and the divisional commissioner confirmed it.
The confirmation remained effective when the High Court suggested that the authorities consider accepting the rival bidder's offer.
The highest offer had not been rejected by the officer conducting the sale.
issues.conclusion: The rival bidder's offer could not be accepted under the next-highest-bid procedure; if the accepted sale was later set aside, the right had to be disposed of afresh under the rules.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 17(4) of the Mysore Excise (Disposal of Privileges of Retail Vend of Liquors) Rules, 1967 permitted consideration of the next-highest bid only when the officer conducting the sale rejected the highest bid. It could not be invoked after the highest offer had been accepted, even if the confirmation was subsequently revised or set aside; in that event a fresh disposal was required.

rule.if: challenge_to_excise_sale_disposal and sale_officer_accepted_highest_offer and highest_offer_not_rejected_at_sale and accepted_sale_later_set_aside

predicates.challenge_to_excise_sale_disposal: A party challenged how the right to retail liquor vending was disposed of after a sale.
predicates.sale_officer_accepted_highest_offer: The officer conducting the sale accepted the highest offer.
predicates.highest_offer_not_rejected_at_sale: The officer conducting the sale did not reject the highest offer at the sale.
predicates.accepted_sale_later_set_aside: The accepted sale or its confirmation was later set aside.

issues.definition: When the highest offer was accepted rather than rejected and the accepted sale is later set aside, the right must be disposed of afresh instead of being awarded to the next-highest bidder under the rejected-bid procedure.
